title: Asynchronous Span-Gate and Batched Metric Writer Refactor
creator: Sofia Chen
description:
Background:
The runtime's current synchronous trace export and metric flush paths are a frequent source of transient heap pressure and CPU spikes under bursty workloads. These spikes translate into higher p95/p99 inference latencies and occasional OOMs in dense multi-tenant processes. Recent incidents (see linked Grafana traces) show the telemetry writer occasionally blocking request workers for up to 120ms during export bursts.

Goal:
Refactor the telemetry ingestion stack to decouple request-critical paths from exporter IO. Deliver an asynchronous "span-gate" (bounded in-process queue + worker pool) and a batched metric writer that aggregates and coalesces high-cardinality labels before export. Target outcomes: reduce 99th-percentile request tail latency by >=15%, reduce telemetry-induced GC pauses, and decrease telemetry CPU overhead by ~20%.

Scope and Non-Goals:
- In scope: tracing ingestion path (span creation -> local queue -> exporter), metric emission path (counter/gauge/histogram buffering + batching), sampling hook integration, graceful shutdown flushing, and feature flags for rollout.
- Out of scope: replacing external exporters (OTLP backend) or long-term storage retention changes. This ticket does not change how customers consume exported telemetry.

Design overview:
1) Span Gate: introduce an async buffer (ring buffer with configurable size and backpressure policy). Producers enqueue span payloads; background workers serialize and export in batches. Backpressure policy options: drop-old, drop-new, and block-when-full (configurable per deployment tier).
2) Batching and Aggregation: group spans/metrics by exporter destination and schema version to maximize exporter throughput. Metric writer will coalesce label sets for frequently-emitted ephemeral labels (session ids, ephemeral host tags) via a TTL-based cache before sending.
3) Sampling and Enrichment: integrate existing sampling plugin so the span-gate can drop spans early when sampling indicates. Enrichment (span attributes added by request handling code) must remain synchronous to preserve attribution; we will enforce a small attribute size limit and serialize asynchronously.
4) Graceful drain & observability: on shutdown or config change we drain buffers with a configurable timeout and emit an internal telemetry event for dropped items. Add exporter queue length, queue overflow count, worker latency histogram, and export error rate metrics and dashboards.

Safety & rollout plan:
- Feature-flagged behind "async_telemetry_v2" with three modes: off, shadow (async path runs but export still mirrors sync path), and on.
- Dark launch in a limited Dedicated cohort for 48h, compare p95/p99 and telemetry loss metrics.
- Canary rollout to 10% of hosts for 72h, then 50%, then 100% if no regressions.
- Rollback: flip feature flag to off; workers will attempt a final drain for 30s before process exit.

Success criteria (observable):
- p99 request latency caused by exporter stalls reduced by >=15% in canary tenants.
- Export queue occupancy remains <60% under 95th percentile load.
- Export error rate no worse than baseline (+1%).

Testing strategy:
- Unit tests for ring buffer semantics (drop/new/block), worker pool failure modes, and graceful drain.
- Load tests: synthetic 100k req/s workload with high-cardinality attributes and validate no increase in request tail latency.
- Chaos: kill exporter connections mid-batch, verify bounded memory and correct drop/error metrics.

Trade-offs and known risks:
- Risk: async path can drop spans if operator chooses drop-new/old policy; must be documented and surfaced to customers.
- Risk: slightly delayed telemetry visibility (tens to hundreds of ms) — acceptable for most observability needs but documented as a change.
- Risk: added complexity in buffering code; mitigate via clear tests, strict invariants, and a single library used across services.

Implementation notes and milestones:
- Phase 1 (2 weeks): implement ring buffer + single worker + metrics; unit tests; local benchmark.
- Phase 2 (2 weeks): add batching/aggregation and sampling hook integration; dark-launch in Dedicated.
- Phase 3 (1 week): canary rollout and metrics dashboards; prepare rollback automation.
- Phase 4 (contingent, 1 week): tune defaults, document, and merge to release branch runtime-1.20.

Observability & dashboards:
- New Grafana: exporter_queue_length, exporter_overflow_count, exporter_worker_latency_ms (histogram), exporter_error_rate.
- Update existing request-latency dashboard to attribute stalls to telemetry backpressure via a new trace-level tag.

Docs and links:
Design doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/RUNTIME/Asynch-Span-Gate-Design
PR (work-in-progress): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/3241
Load test dashboard: https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/abcd1234/latency-overview?orgId=1

Notes on compatibility:
We will maintain OTLP/OTel semantic compatibility; exporters should not require changes. The aggregator will respect exporter batching semantics and use the same protocol endpoints.

Open questions:
- Default queue size and backpressure policy for Hosted tenants vs Dedicated? Proposal: hosted = drop-old with conservative size (64k spans), dedicated = block-when-full with larger buffer (256k).
- Should we expose overflow count and policy per-customer in Console? (UX ask for follow-up ticket)
